name: Wettin
summary: Lineage that ruled Meissen, Thuringia and Saxony from the 12th century to 1918. In 1485 it was divided into the Ernestine and Albertine branches; the Albertines were electors of Saxony and, in the 18th century, kings of Poland.
origin: The lineage takes its name from Wettin Castle, next to the Saale. Conrad the Great gathered in the 12th century the Eastern Marque, Lower Lusacia and Meissen, and his successors were margraves of Meissen. In 1264 Henry the Illustrious received the landgraviate of Thuringia.
history: In 1423 King Sigismund granted Frederick IV of Meissen the electorate and duchy of Saxony-Wittenberg, and from then on Frederick I of Saxony. His grandchildren Ernesto and Albert divided the domains in 1485. The Ernestine elector Frederick the Wise protected Luther; his nephew John Frederick, defeated at Mühlberg (1547), lost the electorate, which Charles V gave to his Albertine cousin Maurice.
legacy: The Albertin electors ruled Saxony until the end of the Empire. Frederick Augustus I was elected king of Poland in 1697 as Augustus II, and his son Augustus III reigned in the Commonwealth until 1763. Ernestine branches formed the Saxon duchies of Thuringia, and the house reigned in Saxony until 1918.

name: Saboya
summary: An alpine house whose branches link the medieval counties, the duchy and the Mediterranean crowns.
origin: The house was formed around alpine domains that grew through inheritance, concessions and marriages. Its dynastic identity survived changes in rank and heritage distribution.
history: The descendants of Thomas I were distributed between the condal line and the estates of his brothers. Later, weddings with Burgundy, Cyprus, France and the Habsburgs expanded their network. The ducal elevation of 1416 and the move of the capital to Turin changed its political position.
legacy: The ducal branch reached the crowns of Sicily and Sardinia. In 1831 the Sardinian succession passed to Carlos Alberto of Savoy-Carignano: a collateral branch of the same family.

name: Lusignan
summary: Lords of Poitou who, on the back of the Crusades, ruled in Jerusalem, Cyprus for almost three centuries and in Cilician Armenia in the 14th century.
origin: The lineage took the name of the castle of Lusignan, in Poitou. Its lords were counts of La Marche and, by the marriage of Hugo X to Isabella of Angoulême, widow of John without Land, also of Angulema.
history: Guy of Lusignan married Sibila, heiress of Jerusalem, and was king from 1186. After losing the kingdom to Saladin, he bought Cyprus from the Templars. His brother Amalaric received the Cypriot crown from Emperor Henry VI and was also king of Jerusalem for his marriage to Elizabeth. Hugo III reunited the two crowns in 1269.
legacy: A branch reigned in Cilician Armenia from 1342 until the fall of Sis in 1375. James II, the last male king, married the Venetian Catherine Cornaro. After the death of her son James III, Catherine ruled under the tutelage of Venice, to which she ceded the island in 1489.

name: Estuardo
summary: Senescales of Scotland, who became kings in 1371, the Stuarts inherited England and Ireland in 1603 and ruled, with the interruption of the Republic, until Anne's death in 1714.
origin: The name comes from the position of senescal (steward) the family held at the Scottish court. Walter Stewart married Marjorie, daughter of Robert I Bruce, and his son Robert II ascended the throne in 1371 upon the extinction of the Bruce.
history: The 15th-century Scottish kings, several of whom were crowned as children, faced a powerful nobility. James IV died at Flodden (1513) against England. Mary Stuart, daughter of James V, lost the throne in 1567. Her son James VI, great-grandson of Margaret Tudor, sister of Henry VIII, inherited the English crown of Elizabeth I in 1603 and united the crowns in his person.
legacy: Charles I was executed in 1649 and the monarchy returned with Charles II in 1660. Catholic James II was deposed in 1688 in favour of his daughter Mary II and William of Orange. The Union of 1707 created Britain under Anne, and upon her death the Act of Establishment carried the crown to the Hanovers, excluding the Catholic Stuart.

name: Basarab
summary: The ruling house of Valaquia was divided into rival lines and linked to the Moldovan court.
origin: The Basarab ruled Wallachia through various branches that competed for the throne. The changes of the prince, depositions and restorations marked its history.
history: Vlad Dracul was the father of Vlad Călugărul, whose descendants continued with Radu the Great and Mircea Ciobanul. Mircea married Chiajna Rareș, from Moldova. His son Petru ascended the throne as a minor and ruled under his mother's political leadership.
legacy: The boyars and Ottoman authority conditioned access to the throne and restoration of the princes. The marriage of Mircea and Chiajna maintained the ties between the courts of Wallachia and Moldova.

name: Hesse
summary: The landgraviate of Hesse grew up among inheritance, family divisions and religious alliances that placed it at the center of imperial politics.
origin: The house descends from Henry, son of Sophia of Brabante and grandson of St. Elizabeth of Hungary. The war for the succession of the Ludovingians separated Hesse from Thuringia in the 13th century. Marburg and Kassel became their main centres of power.
history: Philip I, called the Magnanimous, adopted the Reformation and was one of the leaders of the League of Esmalcalda. His defeat of Charles V limited his imperial position. On his death in 1567 he divided the estate among four sons, originating from the landgraviates of Kassel, Darmstadt, Marburg and Rheinfels.
legacy: Kassel and Darmstadt were the longest-lasting lines. Their confessional differences and hereditary claims fueled conflicts during the Thirty Years' War. The marriages of his princesses linked the family to Russia, Prussia, Savoy and other European courts. The plurality of branches gave continuity to the house during the political transformation of the Empire.

name: Holstein-Gottorp
summary: A branch of Oldburgh that arose from the partition of Schleswig and Holstein came to the Swedish and Russian monarchies.
origin: Adolf, son of Frederick I of Denmark, received in the partition of 1544 a part of Schleswig and Holstein. Gottorf Castle was his residence and gave the branch its name. The ducal domains were intermingled with those of other family lines.
history: The dukes developed a court of considerable artistic and scientific activity. Their alliances with Sweden put them up against the Danish kings. Denmark occupied its share of Schleswig during the Great Northern War, while the family retained their rights and possessions in Holstein.
legacy: Charles Frederick's marriage to Anna Petrovna, daughter of Peter the Great, opened the Russian succession to his son Peter III in 1762. Another line reached Sweden with Adolfo Federico in 1751 and continued with Gustav III and Gustav IV Adolfo. The house thus linked the territorial disputes of the Baltic with two great crowns.

name: Piast
summary: The first Polish dynasty, from Miecislaus I to Casimir III the Great, whose branches continued to rule duchies in Silesia and Mazovia for centuries.
origin: Miecislaus I accepted Christianity in 966 and Bolesław the Pious I was crowned king in 1025. From 1138 onwards the kingdom was divided between the sons of Bolesław the Pious III into regional duchies, and royal dignity was suspended for almost two centuries.
history: Premislao II was crowned king in 1295, but was assassinated the following year. Ladislaus I the Short reunified much of the kingdom and was crowned in Krakow in 1320. His son Casimir III the Great codified laws, founded the University of Krakow (1364) and extended the kingdom into Ruthenia.
legacy: Casimir died without a son in 1370 and the crown passed to his nephew Louis of Anjou, and then to the Jagellons. The Silesian branches of the Piast, such as the Dukes of Świdnica or of Brzeg, continued until 1675, mostly under Bohemian sovereignty.

name: Montfort-Bretaña
summary: The Breton branch of the Montfort went from disputing the duchy to maintaining it for several generations, until Anne of Brittany.
origin: John de Montfort was the son of Arthur II of Brittany and Yolanda de Dreux. His line was part of the Dukes of the House of Dreux, of Capetian descent, and was named after the county of Montfort inherited from Yolanda.
history: John claimed the duchy in 1341. His wife Joan of Flanders defended his cause and that of his son. After John IV's victory, the continuity passed to his sons and grandsons. Marriages with Joan of Navarre, Margaret of Orleans and Margaret of Foix extended the ties of the Breton court.
legacy: Francis II left Anne as heiress. His marriages with Charles VIII and Louis XII linked the duchy to the French monarchy. Claudia, Ana's daughter, extended the transmission. After the deaths of both, the union of 1532 incorporated Brittany into the kingdom of France with guarantees for its institutions.

name: Hannover
summary: The Hanoverian branch of the Welf reunited the German electorate with the British crown through a parliamentary succession.
origin: The house came from the Dukes of Brunswick-Luneburg. The line of Calenberg fixed its court at Hannover and Ernesto Augusto received electoral dignity in 1692. His marriage to Sophia of the Palatinate, granddaughter of James I of England, opened a succession route to the British Isles.
history: The Act of Establishment of 1701 reserved the British succession to Sofia and her Protestant descendants. After her and Queen Anne died in 1714, George Louis of Hannover became George I of Great Britain. George II and George III inherited both positions.
legacy: The governments of Great Britain and Hanover retained their own administrations and territorial interests under one sovereign. British involvement in European wars was conditioned by that connection. The personal union lasted until 1837, when Victoria succeeded in the United Kingdom and Ernesto Augustus inherited Hannover according to his successive rules.

history: Arnaldo Roger I and Ramon Roger I were his successors. Sibila, daughter of Arnaldo Roger, inherited at the end of the 13th century and married Hugo de Mataplana. His descendants gathered the barony of Mataplana with the condal heritage and participated in campaigns of the Crown of Aragon.
legacy: In the 15th century, Hugo Roger III led forces opposed to John II during the Catalan civil war. The resistance continued after the capitulation of Pedralbes. His wife Catalina Albert supported the defense of Valencia d'Àneu until 1491. The confiscation and transfer of the domains to the Cardona put an end to the rule of the comital line and gave way to the marquessate of Pallars.

name: Saluzzo
summary: An Alpine lineage that defended its marquise between the pressures of Savoy and French protection.
origin: The marquis descended from Manfredo, son of Bonifacio del Vasto. The distribution of the family heritage and the development of Saluzzo as a political centre shaped a territorial house of its own.
history: Beatrice of Savoy connects Manfred III and Thomas I with Sicily. In the 15th century, Ludwig I's marriage to Elizabeth of Montferrat linked the Alpine houses back together. Louis II and Margaret of Foix-Candale reinforced the French orientation.
legacy: Disputes between the sons of Ludwig II weakened the marquessate. France imposed its rule in 1548; the territory passed to Savoy by the Treaty of Lyon of 1601.

name: Romanov
summary: The Romanovs left the Moscow nobility to rule a state that became the Russian Empire.
origin: The family took its name from Roman Zakharyin-Yuriev. His daughter Anastasia married Ivan IV, which linked the lineage with the last Rurikid tsars. After the Time of Troubles, the Zemsky Sobor elected Tsar Michael Fiodorovich in 1613.
history: Miguel and his son Alejo rebuilt the authority of the state. Patriarch Filareto, Michael's father, played a decisive role in the early years. Peter I reformed the army and administration, founded St. Petersburg and assumed the imperial title in 1721 after the victory over Sweden.
legacy: The 18th-century succession included palace coups and governments by several empresses. Isabel Petrovna was the last sovereign born in the line of Peter I. With Peter III, son of Anna Petrovna and a duke of Holstein-Gottorp, the Holstein-Gottorp-Romanov line was started in 1762. The continuity of the family name accompanied this transmission through the female line.

name: Este
summary: The Este ruled over Ferrara, Modena and Reggio and developed one of the most influential courts of Renaissance Italy.
origin: The family took its name from the town of Este, in the Veneto. Its branches extended their holdings throughout northern Italy; another line, descended from Azzo II, originated the younger house of the Welf. The Este established their lordship in Ferrara during the 13th century.
history: Borso obtained the titles of duke of Modena and Reggio and then of Ferrara. Hercules I reinforced the capital with a major urban expansion. His sons linked the family to Mantua and Milan, while Alfonso I married Lucrezia Borgia and participated in the Italian wars.
legacy: Alfonso II died without children in 1597. The papacy rejected Cesare d'Este's succession to Ferrara and recaptured the city in 1598. The family kept Modena and Reggio, imperial fiefs, and moved their court, collections and archives there. These domains sustained the continuity of the house for centuries afterwards.

name: Babenberg
summary: The house that ruled the Austrian march from 976 turned its heritage into a duchy and united Austria with Styria before the succession crisis of 1246.
origin: The Babenbergs came from the high Bavarian nobility. Its genealogical relationship with the former counts of Bamberg is disputed. Its Austrian rule began with Leopold I in 976.
history: The family strengthened its position through ties with the Salians, the Hohenstaufen, Hungary and Byzantium. Leopold VI united Austria and Styria, established religious foundations, and participated in imperial politics. His daughter Constance linked with the Wettin of Meissen; his son Frederick II inherited the duchies in 1230.
legacy: Frederick died in 1246 and left the succession rights in the hands of his relatives when the male ducal line became extinct. The dispute over this inheritance preceded the rule of Otakar II and, later, the establishment of the Habsburgs in Austria.
